name: Dante
lede: Dante is a near-black purple recorded in a 1930 color dictionary, with no documented origin for its name.

sections.title: A name with no recorded origin
sections.body:
Dante is a very dark purple-black, #3E2C3A, that appears in our sources only in Maerz and Paul's 1930 *Dictionary of Color*, which dates the name to 1922 and files it on plate 47 [1]. Who first used it, and for what, is undocumented. None of the color books we checked defines it, and none says the shade was named for the poet Dante Alighieri [2]. A link to the poet's dark wood and underworld would be a guess, and no source we have makes it [2].

Our library files it under fashion and textiles, the field in which Maerz and Paul recorded it [1].

sections.title: What the poet did say about color
sections.body:
The books do record real connections between Dante and color, though not to this swatch [3][4]. Gage reports that Dante revived a seven-colour theory of the rainbow in the *Divine Comedy*, and even treated the fainter second bow as a reflection, and so an inversion, of the first [3]. Gage also notes that Dante mentions two miniaturists whose works are not known today [4]. Both are about light and color in the poem, not about a dark purple.

A painter later took the subject back. Delacroix's *Barque of Dante* of 1822 is said to have been the first major painting in which he applied the idea of rainbow colors held in drops of water, here the drops on a torso [5]. The source is Andrieu's account, which may have come from Delacroix himself [5]. Dante Gabriel Rossetti belonged to the Pre-Raphaelites, whose demand for vibrant color caused an uproar in the British art world of the 1850s [6]. These are the poet's color connections, and they do not decide what the dark swatch is named for.

sections.title: What the swatch is
sections.body: On a screen Dante reads as a blackish aubergine: lightness 21, little chroma, and a hue at the purple end [1]. Its nearest named colors are [[poppy-purple]] and [[windsor]], both within about four units, then [[romanesque]] and [[dusty-aubergine]] at 4.5 [7]. [[aubergine]] itself is a lighter, more saturated cousin, 12.7 units away [1]. A true [[dark-purple]] is bluer, and [[raisin-black]] is browner. The color closest to a pure black in this group is [[pale-black-shade]], at 6.0 units [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Dante is an uncommon color in the archive. It appears in 178 of 23,781 paintings, 0.75 percent, above 61 percent of the named colors, as photographed [8]. Within a painting it most often plays a shadow, in 34 percent of the 116 paintings where our within-painting lens finds it [8]. That fits its value: it is a dark that sits in the deepest parts of a picture.

It peaks in the 1900s, in 14 of 1,674 paintings, 0.8 percent and 1.4 times the baseline of the same museums [8]. The first match is a painting by Gentile da Fabriano of 1423, 507 years before the name appears in Maerz and Paul, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment or dye [8]. The plant sources in Werner's 1821 nomenclature that sit nearest are a dark purple scabious, known as Musk Flower, at 5.8 units, and the sweet-scented violet at 6.7 [7]. Look for the color in the shadow of a dark velvet, or in an old varnished portrait where black has aged toward purple.

openers: The color Dante has no recorded origin: nobody says whether the poet had anything to do with it.
